Why Slots and Table Games Don't Count the Same Toward a Bonus

Published September 8, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A casino bonus usually advertises one clean number: a $200 bonus with a 20x wagering requirement means $4,000 in total wagering before the money is yours to withdraw. What that headline number doesn't tell you is that not every dollar you bet actually counts toward it the same way. A $10 blackjack hand might contribute as little as $1 toward that requirement, while a $10 slot spin often contributes the full $10. That gap — called the contribution rate — is one of the least explained parts of casino bonus terms, and it's the difference between a wagering requirement that takes a weekend to clear and one that takes considerably longer than most players expect.

What a contribution rate actually is

A contribution rate is the percentage of a wager that counts toward clearing a bonus's wagering requirement, and it's set independently for each game or category of games. A slot with a 100% contribution rate means every dollar wagered counts as a full dollar toward the requirement. A table game with a 10% contribution rate means a $10 bet only counts as $1 toward that same target. The bonus terms almost always disclose contribution rates somewhere, but they're typically buried in a separate section from the headline wagering multiplier, which is exactly why so many players clear a bonus far more slowly than they expected, or discover midway through that their favorite game barely moves the number at all.

Why games don't contribute equally in the first place

Contribution rates exist because operators are managing their own financial exposure, not because of any regulatory requirement to weight games a particular way. Games with a low house edge — blackjack played with correct strategy, baccarat's banker bet, certain video poker paytables — are cheap for a skilled player to grind through in terms of expected loss. If those games counted at 100%, a player could theoretically clear a large bonus while giving up very little in expected value along the way, which defeats the point of the bonus from the operator's perspective. Slots, by contrast, typically carry a higher built-in house edge and more volatility, so operators are comfortable letting slot wagers count in full — the math already favors the house more per dollar wagered, so there's less risk in letting that wagering clear the requirement quickly.

The pattern to remember: contribution rates track house edge almost directly — the lower a game's edge, the lower its contribution rate tends to be, because operators are pricing in how cheaply a sharp player could otherwise clear the requirement.

Typical contribution rates by game type

Exact numbers vary by operator and even by specific game within a category, so the table below reflects common ranges rather than a universal standard — always check the specific terms attached to any individual bonus.

Game typeTypical contribution rangeWhy
Online slots90%–100%Higher built-in house edge, favors the operator regardless of pace
Video poker10%–25%Optimal-strategy paytables can carry a very low edge
Blackjack5%–20%Basic strategy pushes the house edge close to even
Baccarat (banker bet)5%–15%One of the lowest house edges of any casino game
Roulette10%–25%Moderate house edge, but low variance on outside bets makes it grindable
Live dealer gamesOften 0%–20%Real-time table games carry similar grind-resistant math to their RNG counterparts

Working through the math on a real example

Say a player accepts a $100 bonus with a 25x wagering requirement, meaning $2,500 in qualifying wagers is needed before the bonus funds convert to withdrawable cash. If that player exclusively plays slots at a 100% contribution rate, they need to wager $2,500 in total slot bets to clear it. If they instead play blackjack at a 10% contribution rate, a $10 wager only counts as $1 toward the requirement, meaning they'd need $25,000 in actual blackjack wagering to hit the same $2,500 threshold. That's not a small gap — it's a tenfold difference in how much money needs to move through the table before the requirement clears, even though the bonus amount and multiplier look identical on the surface. This is the single biggest reason two players can have wildly different experiences with what looks like the same offer.

When a game is excluded from wagering entirely

Some games don't contribute at all, and playing them while a bonus is active doesn't just clear the requirement slowly — it doesn't move it at all. This is common for progressive jackpot slots in some jurisdictions, certain low-edge side bets, and occasionally an operator's entire live dealer category. A handful of operators go further and specify that wagering on excluded games while a bonus balance is active can void the bonus altogether, so it's worth confirming which games are excluded outright, not just which ones contribute at a reduced rate, before playing anything other than the games clearly meant for clearing the offer.

What to actually check in the terms before you opt in

The wagering multiplier gets all the attention because it's the headline number, but the contribution table is what actually determines how long clearing a bonus will take for the games you actually enjoy playing. Before opting into any offer, it's worth locating the specific contribution percentage for your preferred game type, not just the overall multiplier, and doing the same math shown above with your own typical bet size. A bonus that looks generous on a slots-only contribution schedule can turn into a much longer grind — or a mathematically unfavorable one — if your game of choice sits in the 5%–15% range. None of this makes bonus offers worthless, but treating the advertised multiplier as the whole story is how players end up surprised by how little progress they've made after a long session.

Frequently asked questions

Why don't casinos just let every game count at 100%?

Because low house-edge games like blackjack and baccarat could then be used to clear a bonus while giving up very little in expected value, which undermines the financial purpose of offering the bonus in the first place.

Where do I find a game's exact contribution rate?

It's almost always listed in the bonus terms and conditions, usually in a separate table or section from the headline wagering multiplier — look for a heading like "game contributions" or "weighting" rather than assuming it's stated near the bonus amount itself.

Does the contribution rate change once I've accepted the bonus?

It shouldn't change mid-offer under normal terms, but rates can differ between promotions even at the same operator, so a contribution rate you remember from a previous bonus isn't guaranteed to apply to a new one.

Are live dealer games treated the same as their RNG equivalents?

Not always. Because live dealer tables carry the same grind-resistant math as their digital counterparts, many operators apply similarly low contribution rates, and some exclude live dealer play from bonus wagering entirely — check the terms rather than assuming parity with the RNG version.
